Chapter 3: Commitment, Consistency, and the Drive to Align Actions.
Let’s dive into one of the most powerful forces shaping how we behave—the need to look and feel consistent. Have you ever noticed how, once you make a decision or take a stand on something, there’s this pull to keep acting in line with that choice? It’s not just about what others expect from you; it’s about how you see yourself, too.
Picture someone making a public promise to support a cause. Even if it’s just a small comment or a casual “sure, I’m in,” suddenly, there’s this internal push to actually follow through. Why? Because keeping that commitment isn’t just about living up to what you said, it’s about protecting your own self-image. You want to feel like you’re someone who sticks to their word.
Here’s something to pay attention to—the need for consistency can be so strong, it sometimes overrides common sense. People will hang onto a decision, even when it’s clear that changing course would make more sense. Why? Because flip-flopping feels uncomfortable. Both we and others tend to see inconsistency as a weakness. So, to avoid looking unreliable, we double down—even if it means sticking with a bad plan.
Now, if you’re wondering how this plays out in real life, think about persuasion techniques. There’s a classic one called the “foot-in-the-door” method. It starts with a tiny ask—something so small, it’s easy to say yes. But once you’ve agreed, the next, bigger request feels much harder to turn down. You already said yes once, so your mind nudges you to stay consistent.
For example, a charity might first ask you to sign a simple petition. That’s a low-effort commitment. But later, when they come back for a donation, you’re way more likely to give. That first, tiny step sets the stage for much bigger actions down the line.
You’ll see this in consumer behavior, too. If someone publicly endorses a product or brand, they’re more likely to keep buying it—even if something better comes along. That first endorsement creates a little psychological investment, and letting go of it just feels wrong.
Here are a few ways you’ll spot this principle in action:
Starting with a small request to open the door for bigger ones... Encouraging people to make public or written commitments so they’re more likely to follow through... And framing choices in a way that reminds someone of what they’ve already committed to.
Of course, while consistency is usually a good thing—helping us build trust and stick to our promises—it’s easy to get caught up and become stubborn. Sometimes, the best move is to pause and ask yourself, “Does this commitment still make sense, now that I know more?” And before making public promises, it’s smart to take a moment and really think it through.
At its best, consistency brings stability and makes relationships and organizations stronger. It helps us build trust and feel good about ourselves. But true integrity? It means being willing to change course when circumstances change. The real goal is to be consistent with your values—not just with what you’ve done in the past.
